about: Competitive land mines: vendor-neutral success criteria where the Zscaler platform stands apart, each proved by tests in the customer's tenant. 'why' and 'ask' are customer-facing and never name a vendor. 'se' notes are for the SE only: what each competitor's own public documentation says, with sources; stance gap = use it, parity = skip it, strong = avoid it, unknown = test, don't claim.
se_status: From competitors' public docs, researched 2026-10-25. Docs change: re-check a source before quoting it to anyone.

independent.text: CyberRatings 2025 SSE comparative test: Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet and Versa rated Recommended; Cisco, Cloudflare and Skyhigh rated Caution; Netskope and Cato were absent from the report.

differentiators.title: Every port inspected, not just web traffic
differentiators.why: Threats and data move on any port. Inspecting only standard web ports leaves a gap an attacker or a careless app can use.
differentiators.ask: From the endpoint agent, with the configuration you'd ship: show TLS on a non-standard port decrypted and inspected, and non-web traffic logged and controlled.

zscaler.needs: ZIA Advanced Firewall, and Auto Proxy Forwarding for Non-Defined Ports (Advanced Settings) so non-standard-port web traffic goes to the web proxy; Z-Tunnel 2.0 in the forwarding profile.

prisma.note: Their docs say the agent routes all traffic to Prisma Access by default. Don't pick this fight.

netskope.note: Their steering doc recommends web-only steering (HTTP/HTTPS) for most customers and All Traffic when Cloud Firewall is subscribed. Check whether the quote includes Cloud Firewall.

cisco.note: The roaming module steers web traffic on ports 80/443 to the SWG; all ports need VPN-as-a-service.

cloudflare.note: By default Gateway inspects HTTP only on port 80 (HTTPS on 443 with decryption); other ports need protocol detection with 'inspect on all ports'. Non-HTTP protocols inside TLS bypass network policy filtering.

microsoft.note: The default Internet Access rule tunnels TCP 80 and 443, and the platform assumes standard HTTP/S ports; QUIC isn't supported.

fortinet.note: Default SSL inspection is certificate inspection (not deep). Whether the agent tunnels all ports by default wasn't confirmed.

checkpoint.note: Their docs say the malware engine scans files under 10 MB and only for internet traffic through a browser.

cato.note: The client routes traffic through the tunnel by default. Don't pick this fight.

differentiators.title: Apps outside the browser get the same protection
differentiators.why: Desktop apps, scripts and sync clients move files and data too. Protection that only covers the browser misses them.
differentiators.ask: Run the malware and data-protection tests from a script or desktop app, not a browser, and show the same blocks.

zscaler.needs: Nothing extra: the kit's device tests already run from a script (the POV probe), not a browser.

checkpoint.note: DLP applies only to browser uploads and downloads (native EXE clients aren't supported), and the malware engine covers browser traffic.

fortinet.note: Not researched or couldn't be confirmed: test it, don't claim it.

differentiators.title: Encrypted DNS can't route around policy
differentiators.why: DNS over HTTPS hides lookups from ordinary DNS controls, so a browser setting can quietly bypass DNS security.
differentiators.ask: Turn on DNS over HTTPS in a browser and show the lookup blocked or controlled, with the request logged.

zscaler.needs: DNS Control (the firewall on for the traffic); the kit adds a POV rule blocking DNS over HTTPS. Confirm in your lab first.

microsoft.note: The client doesn't support secure DNS (DoH, DoT, DNSSEC).

netskope.note: DNS Security needs both the Cloud Firewall and DNS licenses: check the quote includes both.

prisma.note: DoH inspection is for listed resolvers, and only the first query of a pipelined connection is inspected; needs DNS Security licensing.

cloudflare.note: DNS is a core strength. Don't pick this fight.

cisco.note: Not researched or couldn't be confirmed: test it, don't claim it.

differentiators.title: Unknown files are held until they're proven safe
differentiators.why: Allowing a never-seen file while it's analyzed means patient zero gets it. Holding it until the verdict stops it the first time.
differentiators.ask: Download a file no one has seen before through the endpoint agent, and show it held until the sandbox verdict, not delivered and checked later.

zscaler.needs: Advanced Cloud Sandbox; a rule with first-time action Quarantine (the kit makes it; Zscaler's predefined quarantine rules ship disabled).

cisco.note: Their docs: Secure Malware Analytics doesn't protect against the first download of a new or unknown malicious file.

prisma.note: Wait-for-verdict handling (up to 100 MB) is documented for explicit-proxy traffic; ask them to show it over the agent tunnel.

fortinet.note: The documented wait-for-results option is the FortiClient endpoint sandbox (files up to 100 MB), not the inline gateway.

microsoft.note: Malware protection on Internet Access comes from a Netskope partner offer that needs TLS inspection.

netskope.note: With Advanced Threat Protection, Netskope holds unknown files until a verdict. Don't use this one.

checkpoint.note: Appears to hold files during emulation. Don't use this one.

cloudflare.note: Holds supported file types behind an interstitial (Enterprise add-on). Don't use this one.

cato.note: Sandbox needs the ATP license; files over 100 MB aren't supported.

differentiators.title: Large files are still inspected
differentiators.why: Attackers and leaks use big files because many products stop scanning at a size limit.
differentiators.ask: Upload a 60 MB file with sensitive data near the end, and download a large file with a test threat inside, and show both caught.

zscaler.needs: DLP engines take files up to 400 MB and scan the first 100 MB of extracted text. Confirm the 60 MB test in your lab first.

cato.note: Inline DLP maximum file size is 50 MB; the sandbox doesn't support files over 100 MB.

cisco.note: AV scans only the first 50 MB; a Cisco announcement recommends blocking uploads over 50 MB because DLP can't scan them.

checkpoint.note: Threat Prevention doesn't inspect encrypted files or files over 10 MB (add a large malware test by hand).

cloudflare.note: AV scanning limit is 100 MB on Enterprise (15 MB Free, 25 MB PAYG); archives over three levels can't be scanned.

prisma.note: Enterprise DLP handles files up to 100 MB depending on the app: a 60 MB test won't separate you. Use 150 MB only if Zscaler passes it in your lab.

differentiators.title: Private apps stay invisible
differentiators.why: An app that can be reached can be attacked. Connecting users to one app, not the network, removes the attack surface and stops lateral movement.
differentiators.ask: Show a user reaching one private app and nothing else on that server or network, with no inbound port open to the internet.

zscaler.needs: Nothing extra: App Connectors connect outbound only, and the POV segment opens only the app's ports.

cloudflare.note: Their docs: by default every enrolled device can connect to a private network published through Cloudflare Tunnel; a catch-all block policy is recommended.

microsoft.note: Quick Access (network-wide) is described as a transition state; check whether the POV uses Quick Access or per-app access.

prisma.note: Service connections give mobile users access to private apps and resources (network-level); check whether the POV uses ZTNA Connector instead.

checkpoint.note: Lists 'full mesh any-to-any connectivity to your private network' as a SASE benefit.

cisco.note: Resource connectors are outbound-only and per-resource; VPN-as-a-service is network-level. Check which the POV uses.

netskope.note: Per-app access with outbound-only publishers. Don't use this one.

cato.note: Per-app Private Access with deny-by-default rules. Don't use this one.

fortinet.note: Not researched or couldn't be confirmed: test it, don't claim it.

differentiators.title: Slow apps traced hop by hop, on every device
differentiators.why: When an app is slow, the question is where: Wi-Fi, ISP, the security cloud or the app. Hop-by-hop paths and device health answer it.
differentiators.ask: For a slow app, show the hop-by-hop path from the user's device to the app with Wi-Fi, CPU and memory, on Windows, macOS and mobile, within the quoted licenses.

zscaler.needs: ZDX is licensed too: compare what each quote includes, not list prices.

prisma.note: ADEM needs its own license and runs on Windows or macOS endpoints only for mobile users.

cato.note: DEM needs a separate license; app performance metrics cover outbound TCP only.

cloudflare.note: DEX traceroute gives hop-by-hop latency and loss but isn't available on Linux or iOS.

netskope.note: DEM is enabled through the sales representative; path depth not confirmed.

cisco.note: Experience monitoring uses the ThousandEyes module; entitlement varies.

fortinet.note: Not researched or couldn't be confirmed: test it, don't claim it.

differentiators.title: AI security proven on their own AI, live
differentiators.why: AI risk is specific: prompt injection on their own apps, sensitive data in prompts, and AI tools nobody approved. It should be shown blocking, not described.
differentiators.ask: Attack your own AI application with prompt injection and data-leak prompts and show each one blocked inline; show sensitive data stopped in a GenAI prompt and an unapproved AI tool isolated.

zscaler.needs: AI Guard for the customer's AI app; ZIA for the GenAI controls.

checkpoint.note: Prompt attack detection for MCP and agent traffic is Early Availability and detect-only: it doesn't block.

prisma.note: Broad AI runtime security (AIRS). Fight on measured results, not features.

netskope.note: AI guardrails, gateway and red teaming are GA. Fight on measured results.

cisco.note: AI Access and AI Defense exist. Fight on measured results.

cato.note: AI security for apps exists (separate SKU). Fight on measured results.

cloudflare.note: Firewall for AI protects apps proxied by Cloudflare; check whether the customer's AI app is.

microsoft.note: Not researched or couldn't be confirmed: test it, don't claim it.

differentiators.title: Same policy on any network, one agent
differentiators.why: Users work from home, hotels and offices. Protection that changes with the network is protection that fails when people travel.
differentiators.ask: Run the same tests on the office network and on home Wi-Fi with no VPN, and show identical results from one agent.

zscaler.needs: Nothing extra: the forwarding profile sets on- and off-network behavior; the kit's profile tunnels both.

netskope.note: On premises, dynamic steering sends cloud apps only by default; All Traffic on-prem needs a backend option enabled by support.

microsoft.note: Check multi-session or VM hosts: the client doesn't support concurrent sessions or hosts that run VMs.
